claims.claim: In qua1-1 stem apices grown on 2.5% agar, cell separations occur primarily longitudinally with a mean gap angle of 91 ± 7° relative to the transverse axis.
claims.source: In the stem apex, we obtained a mean gap angle (θG) of 91 ± 7° (n = 8 samples), relative to the transverse axis of the stem.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative image analysis of cell separation patterns.

claims.claim: In dark-grown qua1-1 hypocotyls grown on 2.5% agar, 135 events of transverse cell separation and only 9 events of longitudinal cell separation were observed.
claims.source: In thirteen images from individual hypocotyls, we counted on average about 11 events of cell separation per image. In total, we found 135 events in which cells had separated along their shared transverse wall, and nine events in which they had separated along their shared longitudinal wall.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by manual counting of cell separation events in confocal images.

claims.claim: In light-grown qua1-1 hypocotyls grown on 2.5% agar, the mean gap angle is 5 ± 30°.
claims.source: When grown on 2.5% agar, transverse gaps were detected in light-grown qua1-1 hypocotyl (Figure 3K). In contrast to dark-grown hypocotyls, we almost only observed slight cell separations in light-grown hypocotyls, as marked by bright propidium iodide staining, consistent with reduced elongation. Because the gaps were much smaller, we could use our pipeline and measured a mean θG of 5 ± 30° (Figure 3K; Figure 1—figure supplement 4, n = 8 samples).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative image analysis shown in Figure 3K and Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: Cell separation orientation in 3-day-old qua1-1 cotyledons shows no preferential orientation.
claims.source: Using our pipeline, we analyzed cell separation orientation, focusing on cotyledons at a very young stage (3-day old) in order to observe very early cell separations before gaps become too large. No preferential gap orientations could be detected (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by image analysis data shown in Figure 4C and statistical testing (Rao's spacing test, p-value=0.5).

claims.claim: The petiole-blade junction in qua1-1 cotyledons exhibits large cell separations when grown on 2.5% agar medium.
claims.source: When growing seedlings on a 2.5% agar medium, while almost no more cell separation could be observed on the cotyledon blade (see Figure 1H and J), the junction between the petiole and the isotropically expanding cotyledon blade exhibited large cell separations (Figure 4D and I).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by observational data shown in Figure 4D and I.

claims.claim: The petiole-blade junction exhibits increased turgor pressure, apparent stiffness, and surface tension compared to the blade.
claims.source: When measuring the mechanical properties of the petiole-blade junction with AFM, we actually found that this region exhibits increased turgor pressure, apparent stiffness and surface tension (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by AFM measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: CMTs at the stem apex are oriented transversely, matching the stress pattern revealed by qua1-1 cell separation patterns.
claims.source: CMTs at the stem apex were oriented transversely, matching the stress pattern revealed by the qua1-1 cell separation patterns (Figure 3D; for plants grown on 2.5% agar medium: Mean θM = 3 ± 26°, Mean anisotropy = 0.20 ± 0.08, R = 0.65, n = 1669 cells in 13 samples).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of CMT orientations shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: In dark-grown hypocotyls, CMTs are highly aligned longitudinally at the bottom part of the hypocotyl.
claims.source: Focusing on the bottom part of the hypocotyl, where cell separation was observed in qua1-1, we observed that CMTs were highly aligned longitudinally in the wild type, when grown in the same conditions as in qua1-1 (Figure 3H; seedlings grown on 2.5% agar medium: Mean θM = 98 ± 6°, Mean anisotropy = 0.47 ± 0.06, R = 0.98, n = 182 cells in 12 samples)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of CMT orientations shown in Figure 3H.

claims.claim: In light-grown hypocotyls, CMTs show a significant bias towards longitudinal orientations.
claims.source: Yet, when taking into account the anisotropy level of the CMT arrays (to put more weight on CMT orientations when anisotropy is high, as done throughout in this article), we revealed a significant bias towards longitudinal CMT orientations, that is parallel to the tensile stress pattern revealed by the cell separations in qua1-1 (Figure 3L, seedling grown on 2.5% agar medium: Mean θM = 113 ± 30°, Mean anisotropy = 0.25 ± 0.10, R = 0.59, n = 606 cells in 11 samples).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of CMT orientations shown in Figure 3L.

claims.claim: CMT arrays reorient circumferentially around ablation sites in wild-type hypocotyls 8 hours after ablation.
claims.source: As expected, reorientation of CMT arrays was observed in hypocotyls 8 hr after ablation, confirming that CMTs can align along maximal tension in hypocotyls too (Figure 5D and E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by observational data from ablation experiments shown in Figure 5D and E.

claims.claim: qua1-1 light-grown hypocotyls display less consistent CMT orientation at the tissue scale compared to wild type.
claims.source: Whereas CMTs looked normal within individual qua1-1 cells, they displayed less consistent orientation at the tissue scale in qua1-1 cells than in the wild type (Figures 3L and 5A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of CMT orientations shown in Figures 3L and 5A.

claims.claim: The mean resultant vector length for CMT orientations is significantly lower in qua1-1 GFP-MBD hypocotyls (0.42 ± 0.23) compared to wild-type GFP-MBD hypocotyls (0.69 ± 0.14) when grown on 1% agar.
claims.source: we found a mean resultant vector length for GFP-MBD samples of 0.69 ± 0.14 and 0.42 ± 0.23 for qua1-1 GFP-MBD and the populations were significantly different (t-test p-value=0.012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis and statistical testing (t-test p-value=0.012).

claims.claim: When grown on 2.5% agar medium, wild-type and qua1-1 mutant hypocotyls exhibit similar CMT behaviors.
claims.source: When grown on 2.5% agar medium, the wild type and qua1-1 mutant hypocotyls exhibited similar CMT behaviors: we found a mean resultant vector length for GFP-MBD (2.5% agar) samples of 0.69 ± 0.15 and 0.65 ± 0.17 for qua1-1 GFP-MBD (2.5% agar) (n = 606 cells in 11 samples and 865 cells in 15 samples, respectively) and the populations were not significantly different (t-test p-value=0.556).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis and statistical testing (t-test p-value=0.556).

claims.claim: CMT reorientation in response to ablation is dramatically reduced in qua1-1 compared to wild type.
claims.source: Strikingly, this response was dramatically reduced in qua1-1 (Figure 5F and G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by observational data from ablation experiments shown in Figure 5F and G.

claims.claim: In wild-type hypocotyls, the mean CMT angle relative to ablation sites shifts from 47 ± 26° at t=0h to 58 ± 25° at t=8h, showing significant reorganization (p-value=0.002).
claims.source: At t = 0 hr, the GFP-MBD line exhibited a mean angle of 47 ± 26° showing an homogeneous distribution and no preferred orientation of the microtubules relative to the ablation site (n = 101 cells in 10 samples; Figure 5H). At t = 8 hr the mean angle shifted to 58 ± 25°, and the distribution exhibited a strong skewing towards the 80 to 90° angles (n = 101 cells in 10 samples; Figure 5I), demonstrating a significant reorganization of the CMT arrays around the ablation site (p-value=0.002).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis and statistical testing (p-value=0.002) shown in Figure 5H and I.

claims.claim: qua1-1 GFP-MBD hypocotyls do not show significant CMT reorganization 8 hours after ablation (p-value=0.186).
claims.source: The qua1-1 GFP-MBD line however, did not show a significant reorganization of its CMT arrays 8 hr after the ablation (Figure 5J and K, Mean angle at t = 0h: 45 ± 26° and t = 8h: 50 ± 26°, n = 107 cells in 10 samples; p-value=0.186).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis and statistical testing (p-value=0.186) shown in Figure 5J and K.

claims.claim: A discontinuous outer wall hampers the ability of CMTs to align with supracellular maximal tension in the epidermis.
claims.source: Overall, these results demonstrate that a discontinuous outer wall hampers the ability of CMTs to align with supracellular maximal tension in the epidermis (Figure 5O).
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results on CMT behavior in qua1-1 mutants with adhesion defects.

claims.claim: The epidermis acts as a load-bearing layer under tension in aerial organs.
claims.source: consistent with the epidermal theory of growth where the epidermis is put under tension through the pressure exerted by inner tissues, and thus is load-bearing for aerial organs (Kutschera and Niklas, 2007; Savaldi-Goldstein et al., 2007; Maeda et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Kutschera and Niklas, 2007; Savaldi-Goldstein et al., 2007; Maeda et al., 2014).

claims.claim: In plants, cell adhesion is achieved through the deposition of a pectin-rich middle lamella between contiguous cell walls.
claims.source: In plants, cell adhesion is achieved through the deposition of a pectin-rich middle lamella between contiguous cell walls (Orfila et al., 2001; Daher and Braybrook, 2015; Willats et al., 2001; Chebli and Geitmann, 2017; Jarvis et al., 2003; Knox, 1992).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claims.claim: Cortical microtubules align along predicted maximal tensile stress direction.
claims.source: CMTs have previously been shown to align along predicted maximal tensile stress direction (Green and King, 1966; Williamson, 1990).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Green and King, 1966; Williamson, 1990).

claims.claim: CMT alignment with maximal tension has been observed in sunflower hypocotyl.
claims.source: Such response was observed in sunflower hypocotyl (Hejnowicz et al., 2000)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Hejnowicz et al., 2000).

claims.claim: CMT alignment with maximal tension has been observed in Arabidopsis shoot apical meristems.
claims.source: Arabidopsis shoot apical meristems (Hamant et al., 2008)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Hamant et al., 2008).

claims.claim: CMT alignment with maximal tension has been observed in Arabidopsis leaves.
claims.source: leaves (Jacques et al., 2013)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Jacques et al., 2013).

claims.claim: CMT alignment with maximal tension has been observed in Arabidopsis cotyledons.
claims.source: cotyledons (Sampathkumar et al., 2014)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Sampathkumar et al., 2014).

claims.claim: CMT alignment with maximal tension has been observed in Arabidopsis sepals.
claims.source: sepals (Hervieux et al., 2016)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Hervieux et al., 2016).

claims.claim: The continuity of the outer epidermal wall may be a key element to propagate tensile stress over several cell files.
claims.source: In plants, the outer epidermal wall is inherited from the zygote and its continuity may be one of the key element to propagate tensile stress over several cell files (Galletti et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Galletti et al., 2016) and is further tested in this study.

claims.claim: Shape-derived stress corresponds to pressure stress calculated based on the assumption that an organ behaves like a pressure vessel.
claims.source: Shape-derived stress, or pressure stress, is calculated based on the assumption that an organ behaves like a pressure vessel, that is like a load-bearing envelope under tension.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established principles of solid mechanics applied to plant tissues.

claims.claim: Growth-derived stress corresponds to mechanical conflicts arising from differential growth rates or directions.
claims.source: Growth-derived stress corresponds to mechanical conflicts arising from differential growth rates or directions ([Rebocho et al., 2017; Thimann and Schneider, 1938; Kutschera, 1992], Figure 3N).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research and illustrated in Figure 3N.

claims.claim: For a cylindrical shape, shape-derived stress results in tension twice as high in the transverse direction than in the longitudinal direction.
claims.source: For a cylindrical shape, this results in a tension twice as high in the transverse direction than in the longitudinal direction (Beer and Johnston, 1992).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established principles of solid mechanics, supported by a citation (Beer and Johnston, 1992).

claims.claim: The qua1 mutant is very sensitive to sucrose in the medium, which leads to metabolic stress and growth arrest.
claims.source: Because the qua1 mutant is very sensitive to sucrose in the medium, which leads to metabolic stress and growth arrest of the seedling (Gao et al., 2008)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Gao et al., 2008).

claims.claim: The quasimodo2 (qua2) mutant displays a comparable cell adhesion defect phenotype to qua1.
claims.source: The quasimodo1 (qua1) and qua2 mutants, respectively mutated in a galacturonosyltransferase and a pectin methyltransferase, are both required for the synthesis of a fraction of the cell wall pectins. They also display a comparable cell adhesion defect phenotype (Bouton et al., 2002; Mouille et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Bouton et al., 2002; Mouille et al., 2007).

claims.claim: Hyperosmotic media can affect membrane tension and molecular effectors of cell migration in animal single cells.
claims.source: Previous work on animal single cells showed that hyperosmotic media can affect membrane tension and thus the molecular effectors of cell migration, like actin filaments, RAC activity or WAVE complex, suggesting that the corresponding mutants could be rescued by a modification of the osmotic conditions of the medium (Batchelder et al., 2011; Houk et al., 2012; Asnacios and Hamant, 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Batchelder et al., 2011; Houk et al., 2012; Asnacios and Hamant, 2012).

claims.claim: Adding sorbitol in growth media is sufficient to rescue defects in yeast endocytic mutants.
claims.source: Consistently, adding sorbitol in growth media is sufficient to rescue defects in yeast endocytic mutants (Basu et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Basu et al., 2014).

claims.claim: Dark-grown hypocotyls display a well-characterized gradient of growth during elongation.
claims.source: To go beyond this qualitative assessment, we next focused on dark-grown hypocotyls, since they display a well characterized gradient of growth during their elongation, in which cells closest to the root (rootward) have already extensively elongated and are undergoing growth arrest, cells more toward the middle are rapidly elongating, and cells at the top (shootward) and in the apical hook are only starting to elongate (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, [Gendreau et al., 1997; Bastien et al., 2016]).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Gendreau et al., 1997; Bastien et al., 2016) and illustrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Light-grown hypocotyls usually reach 1.5 to 2 millimeters in length, in contrast to dark-grown hypocotyls which can reach about two centimeters.
claims.source: when grown in light, hypocotyls usually reach 1.5 to 2 millimeters in length, in contrast to dark-grown hypocotyls which can reach about two centimeters (Gendreau et al., 1997).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Gendreau et al., 1997).

claims.claim: Cotyledon growth occurs mainly in 2D and is rather isotropic.
claims.source: In comparison to stems and hypocotyls, cotyledon growth occurs mainly in 2D and is rather isotropic (Zhang et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Zhang et al., 2011).

claims.claim: The proximal region of leaves exhibits increased mechanical stress-driven planar cell polarity.
claims.source: Interestingly, using the plasma-membrane-associated protein BREVIS RADIX LIKE 2 (BRXL2) as a polar marker, the proximal region of leaves was recently shown to exhibit increased mechanical stress-driven planar cell polarity (Bringmann and Bergmann, 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Bringmann and Bergmann, 2017).

claims.claim: Trichome socket cells exhibit a tensile stress pattern that is consistent with radial cracks around trichomes in qua1-1.
claims.source: Interestingly, in the blade of these leaves, we also observed radial cracks around trichomes, a pattern that is also consistent with the recently identified tensile stress pattern in trichome socket cells (Hervieux et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by observational data and a citation to published research (Hervieux et al., 2017).

claims.claim: Wild-type hypocotyls exhibit strong differences in apparent elastic moduli between transverse and longitudinal anticlinal walls in the epidermis.
claims.source: Using atomic force microscopy, it was previously shown that wild-type hypocotyls exhibit strong differences in apparent elastic moduli between transverse and longitudinal anticlinal walls in the epidermis, whereas overexpression of PMEI significantly reduced such mechanical polarities (Peaucelle et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Peaucelle et al., 2015).

claims.claim: Overexpression of PMEI5 significantly reduces mechanical polarities in hypocotyl anticlinal walls.
claims.source: Using atomic force microscopy, it was previously shown that wild-type hypocotyls exhibit strong differences in apparent elastic moduli between transverse and longitudinal anticlinal walls in the epidermis, whereas overexpression of PMEI significantly reduced such mechanical polarities (Peaucelle et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Peaucelle et al., 2015).

claims.claim: CMTs in dark-grown hypocotyls behave differentially at the inner and outer face of epidermal cells.
claims.source: In dark-grown hypocotyls, previous studies had reported that CMTs behave differentially at the inner and outer face of the epidermal cells of the hypocotyl and also display different responses at the hypocotyl shootward region (where cells are not elongated yet), middle (where cell elongation rate is high) and rootward region (where cell elongation is slowing down) (Chan et al., 2010; Chan et al., 2011; Crowell et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published research (Chan et al., 2010; Chan et al., 2011; Crowell et al., 2011).

claims.claim: CMTs are transversely oriented in the inner face of epidermal cells in dark-grown hypocotyls, promoting anisotropic expansion.
claims.source: In particular, CMTs were shown to be transversely oriented in the inner face of the epidermal cell at most of these stages, promoting the anisotropic expansion of the tissue (Crowell et al., 2011)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Crowell et al., 2011).

claims.claim: CMTs constantly rotate in young hypocotyls until they reach either their transverse or longitudinal orientation.
claims.source: For instance, it had been reported that CMTs constantly rotate in young hypocotyl until they reach either their transverse or longitudinal orientation (Chan et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Chan et al., 2007).

claims.claim: CMTs in light-grown hypocotyls have a rotating behavior.
claims.source: Consistently, CMTs in light grown-hypocotyl have also been described to harbor a rotating behavior (Chan et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Chan et al., 2010).

claims.claim: Mutants in microtubule dynamics or cellulose deposition have not been reported to exhibit adhesion defects.
claims.source: In fact, mutants in microtubule dynamics or cellulose deposition have not been reported to exhibit adhesion defects.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on the absence of reports in the literature.

claims.claim: Actin plays a critical role in tension-induced reinforcement of cell-cell adhesion through its impact on pectin delivery to cell walls.
claims.source: It is therefore more likely that other factors, and most likely actin through its impact on pectin delivery to cell walls (Mathur et al., 2003), plays a critical role in the tension-induced reinforcement of cell-cell adhesion, in parallel to microtubule-driven cell wall reinforcement.
claims.evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from published research (Mathur et al., 2003) and the observations in this study.

claims.claim: DEK1 is required for tensile stress perception via its association with a mechanosensitive Ca2+ channel.
claims.source: Our conclusions also echo the recent analysis of the DEFECTIVE KERNEL 1 (DEK1) protein, which was shown to be required for tensile stress perception via its association with a mechanosensitive Ca2+ channel (Tran et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Tran et al., 2017).

claims.claim: DEK1 RNA interference lines exhibit loss of cell adhesion in their epidermis.
claims.source: Interestingly, DEK1 RNA interference lines exhibit loss of cell adhesion in their epidermis (Johnson et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Johnson et al., 2005).

claims.claim: Plant epidermis requires tensile stress perception.
claims.source: Our finding in qua1 thus allows us to revisit these results, suggesting that plant epidermis requires tensile stress perception
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results on qua1 and the connection to DEK1 function.

claims.claim: Cell-cell adhesion allows tensile stress propagation.
claims.source: and in turn, that cell-cell adhesion allows tensile stress propagation.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental results showing that loss of adhesion in qua1 hampers CMT coordination.

claims.claim: The basement membrane in animals may have a similar role to the outer wall in plants in coordinating supracellular epidermal patterns.
claims.source: While the coordinating role of the outer wall is difficult to match with a comparable structure in animals, the basement membrane may in principle have a similar role, given its continuity and key role in both adhesion and mechanotransduction.
claims.evidence: The claim is speculative, based on comparison between plant and animal systems.

claims.claim: Mechanical forces can be propagated at the speed of sound, like acoustic waves.
claims.source: By definition, mechanical forces can be propagated at the speed of sound, like acoustic waves.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established physical principles.

claims.claim: Cell division stops synchronously in the Drosophila wing disc, possibly due to mechanical force propagation.
claims.source: This may provide close to instantaneous coordinating cues to tissues, as proposed in the Drosophila wing disc where cell division stops synchronously (Shraiman, 2005).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Shraiman, 2005).

claims.claim: A cell would experience different tension levels depending on whether it is separated from or adhering to its neighbors.
claims.source: In other words, a cell would experience different tension level and orientation between a situation where it would be separated from its neighbors (typically, cell shape would be sufficient to prescribe a tensile stress pattern, as in [Sampathkumar et al., 2014]) and a situation where it would still adhere to its neighbors (tensile stress could build up at the outer epidermal wall, to a magnitude higher than cell shape-derived stress, and with a pattern that would depend on tissue shape and differential growth, as in [Hamant et al., 2008; Louveaux et al., 2016]).
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results and supported by citations to published research (Sampathkumar et al., 2014; Hamant et al., 2008; Louveaux et al., 2016).

claims.claim: The anisotropy of CMT arrays was slightly increased at the petiole-blade junction compared to the blade.
claims.source: Interestingly, the mean anisotropy of the CMT arrays was slightly increased at the junction, when compared to the blade, consistent with the measured increased tension and mechanical conflict in that region (Mean anisotropy = 0.08 ± 0.04 (blade) vs. 0.11 ± 0.06 (junction); paired comparisons between blade and junction from each sample revealed a significant difference (always higher in junction) (Wilcoxon-test, p-values<0.05) for 10 out of 12 samples in each condition).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis and statistical testing (Wilcoxon-test, p-values<0.05).

claims.claim: When grown on 2.5% agar medium, the anisotropy of CMT arrays was higher at the junction (0.18 ± 0.09) than in the blade (0.08 ± 0.05).
claims.source: As on 1% agar medium, the anisotropy of the CMT arrays was higher at the junction (0.18 ± 0.09) than in the blade (0.08 ± 0.05). Paired comparisons between blade and junction from each sample revealed a significant difference (always higher in junction) for 12 out of 13 samples in each condition (Wilcoxon-test, p-values<0.001).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis and statistical testing (Wilcoxon-test, p-values<0.001).

claims.claim: The resultant vector length for cell separation angles in cotyledons was 0.07, indicating no preferential orientation.
claims.source: R reached 0.84 and 0.70 for the stem apex and light-grown hypocotyls respectively, whereas R was equal to 0.07 for cotyledons.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of cell separation orientations.

claims.claim: The Rao's spacing test revealed a non-uniform distribution of cell separation angles in stem apices and light-grown hypocotyls (p-value<0.001 for both).
claims.source: This contrasts with the stem apex and the light grown hypocotyl cell separations, for which the test revealed a non-uniform distribution (p-value<0.001 for both).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical testing (Rao's spacing test, p-value<0.001).

claims.claim: The Rao's spacing test showed uniformity of the distribution of cell separation angles in cotyledons (p-value=0.5).
claims.source: the population of angles could be considered uniformly distributed, as assessed using the Rao's spacing test for uniformity (non-parametric test due to the apparent bimodal distribution of the angle population, and adapted for directional data, p-value=0.5, n = 12 samples).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by statistical testing (Rao's spacing test, p-value=0.5).

claims.claim: At the petiole-blade junction in qua1-1 cotyledons, gaps appeared preferentially, but not exclusively, along the longitudinal axis of the petiole with a mean angle of 85 ± 50°.
claims.source: Furthermore, gaps at the junction appeared preferentially, but not exclusively, along the longitudinal axis of the petiole (Figure 4D and I). Our pipeline revealed that cell adhesion defects displayed a mean θG of 85 ± 50° (Figure 4D and I, n = 8 samples).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative image analysis shown in Figure 4D and I.

claims.claim: The resultant vector length for cell separation angles at the petiole-blade junction was 0.21, and the Rao's spacing test showed uniformity (p-value of 0.5).
claims.source: Note however that the resultant vector length R was only equal to 0.21 and the Rao's spacing test showed uniformity of the distribution of angles (p-value of 0.5), which suggest that the bias is weak.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis and statistical testing (Rao's spacing test, p-value=0.5).

claims.claim: The skewness of CMT angle distribution in GFP-MBD hypocotyls at t=8h after ablation was -0.77, significantly different from a normal distribution (p-value=0.002).
claims.source: the skewness was much smaller than in the GFP-MBD line: −0.23 in qua1-1 GFP-MBD t = 8 hr vs. −0.77 in GFP-MBD t = 8 hr (0,08 in qua1-1 GFP-MBD t = 0 hr and −0.04 in GFP-MBD t = 0 hr, Figure 5K). In addition a statistical test comparing the skewness of the distribution to a corresponding normal distribution showed that the population of angles are not significantly skewed in GFP-MBD t = 0 hr, qua1-1 GFP-MBD t = 0 hr and qua1-1 GFP-MBD t = 8 hr (p-value=0.858, 0.718 and 0.255 respectively), while GFP-MBD t = 8 hr shows a significant skewing (p-value=0.002).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis and statistical testing (p-value=0.002) shown in Figure 5K.

claims.claim: The skewness of CMT angle distribution in qua1-1 GFP-MBD hypocotyls at t=8h after ablation was -0.23, not significantly different from a normal distribution (p-value=0.255).
claims.source: the skewness was much smaller than in the GFP-MBD line: −0.23 in qua1-1 GFP-MBD t = 8 hr vs. −0.77 in GFP-MBD t = 8 hr (0,08 in qua1-1 GFP-MBD t = 0 hr and −0.04 in GFP-MBD t = 0 hr, Figure 5K). In addition a statistical test comparing the skewness of the distribution to a corresponding normal distribution showed that the population of angles are not significantly skewed in GFP-MBD t = 0 hr, qua1-1 GFP-MBD t = 0 hr and qua1-1 GFP-MBD t = 8 hr (p-value=0.858, 0.718 and 0.255 respectively)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis and statistical testing (p-value=0.255) shown in Figure 5K.

claims.claim: CMTs align along the local maximum of tension around gaps in qua1-1 GFP-MBD.
claims.source: In many instances the anisotropy of CMT arrays was higher in qua1-1 GFP-MBD and CMTs were somehow oriented following the contours of large gaps, thus apparently following a new tension pattern allowed by the continuity of the cells where they are still adhesive (Figure 5A,L–N).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by observational data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5L–N.

claims.claim: Local cell separations lead to the loss of tissue-scale organization of CMTs in qua1-1.
claims.source: Our analysis thus reveals that local cell separations lead to the loss of the tissue-scale organization of the CMTs that is usually found in the wild-type.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the quantitative analysis of CMT orientations in qua1-1 compared to wild type.

claims.claim: Epidermis continuity is required for supracellular CMT behavior.
claims.source: Therefore, while these data further support a scenario in which epidermis continuity is required for supracellular CMT behavior, the cell-cell separations are too strong to conclude.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results, though the authors note the evidence is not conclusive due to the severity of separations.

claims.claim: Increasing agar concentration is not toxic to cells.
claims.source: Because increasing agar concentration is not toxic to the cell, as shown by propidium iodide staining (see Figure 1G and H), we selected this protocol to alter water potential in the following experiments.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by propidium iodide staining data shown in Figure 1G and H.

claims.claim: The epidermis can osmoregulate efficiently.
claims.source: This suggests that water potential primarily affect internal tissues and/or that the epidermis can osmoregulate efficiently, as already shown before (e.g. [Shabala and Lew, 2002]).
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the AFM measurements and supported by a citation to published research (Shabala and Lew, 2002).

claims.claim: Comparable differences in stiffness to those observed in this study were obtained in other tissues with different growth rates.
claims.source: Although such differences in stiffness may appear small, comparable differences were obtained in other tissues, for example between central and peripheral zone of the shoot apical meristem, where differences in growth rates are of 200% to 300% (Milani et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published research (Milani et al., 2014).

claims.claim: The concentrations of PEG and agar were chosen to maintain growth.
claims.source: Furthermore, the concentrations of PEG and agar were chosen so as to maintain growth; in other words, differences could be stronger for higher concentrations, but these would not be relevant for our study.
claims.evidence: The claim describes the experimental design rationale.

claims.claim: Cells at the shootward portion of dark-grown hypocotyls, where rapid elongation has not started yet, show very few cell separations in qua1-1.
claims.source: Note that cells at the shootward portion of the hypocotyl, where rapid elongation has not started yet, very few cells were separated in qua1-1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F), further supporting the role of anisotropic growth in generating the observed gaps.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by observational data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claims.claim: Among nine events of longitudinal cell separation in dark-grown hypocotyls, seven were related to an adjacent event of transverse cell separation.
claims.source: However, among these nine events, seven were related to an adjacent event of transverse cell separation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D and E), while only two events were strictly longitudinal (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by manual counting of cell separation events shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: No significant differences in gaping pattern were detected between dark-grown qua1-1 and qua1-1 p35S::PMEI5 hypocotyls.
claims.source: Yet, we could not detect significant differences in the gaping pattern between dark-grown qua1-1 and qua1-1 p35S::PMEI5 hypocotyls, further confirming that the gaping pattern primarily results from the tension pattern (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by observational data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: A similar response to that in dark-grown hypocotyls was observed in the qua1-1 PMEI-OE line in light-grown hypocotyls.
claims.source: A similar response was observed in the qua1-1 PMEI-OE line, consistent with the pattern primarily resulting from growth-derived stress, and not from heterogeneities of pectin esterification (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by observational data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The immersion medium had little impact on AFM measurements in the short term.
claims.source: We also confirmed that the immersion medium had little impact on the measurement both in wild type and qua1-1, at least in the short term (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by AFM measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The propidium iodide staining truly reflects cell-cell adhesion defects in qua1-1.
claims.source: Last, to confirm that the propidium iodide staining truly reflected cell-cell adhesion defects, we analyzed the gaps in qua1-1 at different stages with confocal microscopy and, at high resolution, with atomic force microscopy. Our images matched previously published SEM images of qua1-1 mutants (Bouton et al., 2002), with stretched and detached outer walls at the cell-cell junction (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy and AFM data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5, and is consistent with previously published SEM images (Bouton et al., 2002).

claims.claim: Adhesion defects in qua1-1 relate to the tensile status of the tissue.
claims.source: Altogether, these results strongly suggest that adhesion defects in qua1-1 indeed relate to the tensile status of the tissue.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined results of water potential manipulation, AFM measurements, and imaging data.

claims.claim: The physics of pressure vessels has been instrumental in deriving stress patterns in plants.
claims.source: The physics of pressure vessel, and more generally of solid mechanics, has been instrumental in the derivation of stress patterns in plants, very much in the spirit of D'Arcy Thompson's legacy (Thompson, 1917).
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established principles of solid mechanics and a historical citation (Thompson, 1917).

claims.claim: This work formally validates several conclusions from previous computational models and stress patterns deduced from ablation experiments.
claims.source: Our results formally validate several conclusions from previous computational models and stress patterns deduced from ablation experiments.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparison of the current results with previous computational and experimental work.

claims.claim: This work brings further experimental proof of the presence of tissue tension.
claims.source: Incidentally, this work also brings further experimental proof of the presence of tissue tension, building on the initial work by Hofmeister (Hofmeister, 1859) and Sachs (Sachs, 1878).
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results and builds on historical citations (Hofmeister, 1859; Sachs, 1878).

claims.claim: Slight oscillations in growth rate could periodically affect the ratio of shape- and growth-derived stress and trigger the rotating behavior of microtubules in hypocotyls.
claims.source: Although this behavior is still an intriguing phenomenon, it could partly be related to the fact that in this tissue, (transverse) shape-derived and (longitudinal) growth-derived stresses are in competition. Slight oscillations in growth rate (Bastien et al., 2016) could periodically affect the ratio of shape- and growth-derived stress and thus trigger this rotating behavior of the microtubules.
claims.evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the current results and a citation to published research (Bastien et al., 2016).

results.result: Reducing water potential of the growth medium by increasing agar concentration or adding PEG rescues cell adhesion defects in qua1-1 mutants by decreasing epidermal tension without affecting turgor pressure.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C10 provide converging evidence from multiple approaches (PEG treatment, agar concentration, confocal imaging, quantitative image analysis, and AFM measurements) demonstrating that low water potential reduces cell separations in qua1-1. The AFM data (C8-C10) formally demonstrate that outer wall tension decreases by 16-18% while turgor pressure remains unchanged, directly linking water potential manipulation to reduced epidermal tension. Statistical significance is established (C7: p=0.0004), and controls confirm the treatment is not toxic (C78, C86).

results.result: In stem apices, cell separations in qua1-1 occur longitudinally (mean angle 91±7°), revealing transverse maximal tension consistent with shape-derived stress in a cylindrical pressure vessel, and CMT orientations in wild-type match this pattern.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C12 demonstrate that low water potential rescues meristem phenotypes and allows quantification of gap patterns showing longitudinal separations (91±7°). Claim C18 shows CMTs orient transversely (3±26°) in wild-type stem apices, perpendicular to the gaps as predicted. Claim C40 provides the theoretical framework from solid mechanics. The concordance between gap patterns, CMT orientations, and theoretical predictions strongly supports the conclusion.

results.result: In hypocotyls, cell separations in qua1-1 occur predominantly transversely (135 transverse vs 9 longitudinal events in dark-grown; mean angle 5±30° in light-grown), revealing longitudinal maximal tension consistent with growth-derived stress, and CMTs in wild-type align longitudinally matching this pattern.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C14 provide quantitative data on gap orientations in both dark- and light-grown hypocotyls showing predominantly transverse separations. Claims C19-C20 demonstrate longitudinal CMT alignment in wild-type hypocotyls. Claims C45-C46 and C82-C83 provide context about growth gradients and support the interpretation that growth-derived stress dominates. The manual counting (C13) and automated analysis (C14) converge on the same conclusion, and the CMT data independently confirm the inferred stress pattern.

results.result: In cotyledons, cell separations show no preferential orientation in the blade (R=0.07, p=0.5) but concentrate at the petiole-blade junction where mechanical properties are elevated, suggesting a mechanical conflict zone.
results.evaluation: Claims C15, C68, and C70 provide statistical evidence (Rao's test p=0.5, R=0.07) that blade separations are uniformly distributed. Claims C16-C17 show that the junction exhibits large separations and increased mechanical properties (AFM measurements). Claims C66-C67 demonstrate increased CMT anisotropy at the junction with statistical significance (Wilcoxon test p<0.05 and p<0.001). Claims C71-C72 show weak preferential orientation at the junction (R=0.21, p=0.5). Together, these support the presence of a mechanical conflict zone, though the directional bias is weak.

results.result: Loss of epidermis continuity in qua1-1 mutants hampers supracellular CMT coordination and their ability to reorient in response to ablation, demonstrating that cell-cell adhesion is required for tensile stress propagation.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C24 show reduced CMT coordination in qua1-1 on 1% agar (R=0.42 vs 0.69, p=0.012) that is rescued on 2.5% agar (p=0.556). Claims C21 and C25-C27 demonstrate that CMT reorientation after ablation is dramatically reduced in qua1-1 (p=0.186 vs p=0.002 in WT). Claims C73-C74 provide quantitative skewness analysis supporting this. Claims C75-C77 show that local separations disrupt tissue-scale CMT organization. Claim C28 synthesizes these findings. The convergence of multiple independent measurements (resultant vector length, ablation response, skewness analysis) strongly supports the conclusion.

results.result: Overexpression of PMEI5 in qua1-1 does not alter gaping patterns, indicating that cell separation patterns result from tension rather than pectin esterification heterogeneities.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C85 provide direct experimental evidence from PMEI5 overexpression lines showing no significant differences in gaping patterns compared to qua1-1 alone. This control experiment effectively rules out an alternative explanation (pectin esterification heterogeneity) and supports the tension-based interpretation. The observation is consistent across both dark- and light-grown hypocotyls.

results.result: The qua1-1 mutant, defective in a glycosyltransferase required for pectin synthesis, exhibits cell adhesion defects in the epidermis that preferentially occur at sites of predicted high stress.
results.evaluation: Claim C1 establishes the genetic basis (supported by citations). Claim C2 documents the phenotype across multiple organs. Claim C5 shows preferential separation at neck-lobe junctions consistent with stress patterns. Claims C29-C30 provide the theoretical framework for epidermal tension. Claim C87 validates that propidium iodide staining reflects true adhesion defects through multiple imaging modalities. This establishes the foundational observation for the study.

results.result: CMTs align along maximal tensile stress direction, as previously demonstrated in multiple plant tissues.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C36 are all supported by citations to published research establishing CMT alignment with stress in sunflower hypocotyls, Arabidopsis shoot apical meristems, leaves, cotyledons, and sepals. This provides the established framework that the current study builds upon and validates.

results.result: The continuity of the outer epidermal wall is required for propagating tensile stress across multiple cell files, and cells experience different tension levels depending on adhesion status.
results.evaluation: Claim C37 introduces the hypothesis (supported by citation to Galletti et al., 2016). Claims C60-C61 synthesize the experimental findings showing that epidermis requires stress perception and that adhesion allows stress propagation. Claim C65 articulates the conceptual framework for how adhesion status affects tension. The experimental results from the CMT coordination and ablation experiments (covered in other result groups) provide strong support for these claims.

results.result: Tensile stress patterns in plant tissues can be decomposed into shape-derived stress (from pressure vessel mechanics) and growth-derived stress (from differential growth).
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C40 define the two types of stress with appropriate citations to solid mechanics principles. Claim C89 establishes the historical and theoretical foundation. These claims provide the conceptual framework for interpreting the experimental results and are well-supported by established physics and engineering principles.

results.result: This work formally validates previous computational models and stress patterns deduced from ablation experiments, providing experimental proof of tissue tension.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C91 are synthesis claims supported by the totality of the experimental results. The concordance between gap patterns in qua1-1, CMT orientations in wild-type, and theoretical predictions from solid mechanics provides strong validation. The work builds on historical foundations (Hofmeister, Sachs) and provides direct experimental evidence for tension patterns previously only inferred.

results.result: Hyperosmotic media can rescue mechanical defects in single cells by affecting membrane tension, as shown in animal cells and yeast.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C44 are supported by citations to published research on animal cells and yeast. These provide the conceptual foundation and precedent for the experimental approach used in this study, extending single-cell observations to multicellular plant tissues.

results.result: The epidermis can osmoregulate efficiently, and the observed 15-18% differences in stiffness and tension are biologically meaningful despite appearing small.
results.evaluation: Claim C79 is supported by AFM data and citation to Shabala and Lew, 2002. Claim C80 provides comparative context from other tissues (Milani et al., 2014) showing similar magnitude differences correlate with large growth rate differences. Claim C81 explains the experimental design rationale. Together these address potential concerns about the magnitude of observed effects.

results.result: The proximal region of leaves exhibits increased mechanical stress-driven planar cell polarity, and mechanical polarities in hypocotyls can be modulated by PMEI overexpression.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C51 are all supported by citations to published research (Bringmann and Bergmann, 2017; Hervieux et al., 2017; Peaucelle et al., 2015). These provide additional context and support for the mechanical patterns observed in this study, particularly regarding the petiole-blade junction and the role of pectin esterification.

results.result: CMTs in hypocotyls display complex behaviors including differential orientation at inner and outer faces, regional differences, and rotating behavior.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C55 are all supported by citations to published research (Chan et al., 2007, 2010, 2011; Crowell et al., 2011). These establish the known complexity of CMT behavior in hypocotyls and provide context for interpreting the current results, particularly the observation that light-grown hypocotyls show less consistent CMT alignment than dark-grown ones.

results.result: Actin, rather than microtubules, likely plays the critical role in tension-induced reinforcement of cell-cell adhesion through its impact on pectin delivery.
results.evaluation: Claim C56 is based on absence of reports in the literature, which is weak evidence. Claim C57 is explicitly speculative, based on inference and a single citation (Mathur et al., 2003). While the reasoning is logical, the authors acknowledge this is speculative and no direct experimental evidence is provided in this study. This represents a hypothesis for future work rather than a supported conclusion.

results.result: DEK1 is required for tensile stress perception and exhibits loss of cell adhesion when disrupted, suggesting a link between stress perception and adhesion.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C59 are supported by citations to published research (Tran et al., 2017; Johnson et al., 2005). Claims C60-C61 connect these prior findings to the current results, suggesting that the qua1 phenotype allows revisiting the DEK1 results in a new light. The synthesis is logical and well-supported by the combination of prior work and current findings.

results.result: The basement membrane in animals may play a similar coordinating role to the plant outer wall, and mechanical forces can propagate rapidly like acoustic waves.
results.evaluation: Claim C62 is explicitly speculative, drawing an analogy between plant and animal systems without direct evidence. Claim C63 is a physical principle (supported). Claim C64 is supported by citation (Shraiman, 2005) but represents a proposed mechanism rather than demonstrated fact. These claims are primarily speculative discussion points rather than supported conclusions from the current work.

results.result: Oscillations in growth rate could periodically affect the ratio of shape- and growth-derived stress and trigger rotating behavior of microtubules in hypocotyls.
results.evaluation: Claim C92 is explicitly speculative, proposing a mechanism to explain the previously reported rotating behavior of CMTs in hypocotyls. While the hypothesis is logical and builds on the current results and a citation (Bastien et al., 2016), no direct experimental evidence is provided to test this mechanism. This represents an interesting hypothesis for future work.
